screens.narratorSegment: In cloud billing, visibility is the first line of defence. In this lesson you will learn what a Snowflake Resource Monitor does, how credits measure cost across compute, storage and cloud services, and why combining quotas with automated triggers prevents runaway spend. We will ground this with concrete S Q L commands you can run, a short simulation you can reproduce in a sandbox, and the ACCOUNT_USAGE views you use to analyze consumption. You’ll see how a tiered approach — account-level monitors plus targeted warehouse monitors — gives both budget-level protection and workload-level control. A practical example: if a long-running ETL keeps an X-SMALL warehouse running, a daily quota and a suspend trigger stop further credits from accruing until someone reviews the workload. Common pitfalls we’ll avoid include relying only on email notifications, using overly large quotas that are ineffective, and failing to test suspend actions in non-production. By the end you will be able to create a monitor, assign it, read metering history, and choose sensible triggers. Consider: what workload in your environment would you protect first and why?

screens.title: What is a Resource Monitor?
screens.narratorSegment: A Resource Monitor is a Snowflake object that measures credit consumption and enforces controls when thresholds are reached. Think of it as an automated budget guardrail: you set a CREDIT_QUOTA for a time period, and the monitor counts consumed credits against that quota. The practical reason this exists is billing behavior — compute credits accrue while warehouses run, storage grows over time, and cloud services use credits for account-level operations. A concrete example helps. Imagine a development warehouse that accidentally stays active overnight during a large data load. A daily resource monitor with a small CREDIT_QUOTA will notify at intermediate percentages and then suspend the warehouse when the quota is reached, halting further cost accrual. One common misconception is that resource monitors stop all billing automatically across storage and services; they primarily control compute consumption for assigned warehouses or the account level via SUSPEND actions. Storage and cloud services still accrue unless you explicitly manage those costs separately. Takeaway: resource monitors translate credit tracking into enforced actions, but they must be combined with usage analysis and design to be effective. Which small workload in your environment would you protect first and why?

keyIdea.title: Monitor = automated budget guardrail
keyIdea.text: Resource monitors measure credits and execute triggers to notify or suspend workloads when thresholds are met.

content.html:
Core Concept › What is a Resource Monitor?
Definition and purpose
A monitor tracks credits and enforces quota-based actions to limit compute spend. It is used to prevent unexpected billing and to formalize budgets.
Why it matters
Transforms passive metering into active controls that stop runaway queries or forgotten warehouses.
Common misconception
Monitors do not automatically reduce storage costs; they primarily control compute via warehouse suspension and account-level limits.
Concrete example
A daily monitor with CREDIT_QUOTA = 5 will notify at intermediate thresholds and suspend the warehouse when the quota is reached, stopping further compute credits for that period.
Analogy
Treat the monitor like a prepaid data cap. You set how many credits are allowed for a period, and the system enforces that cap so you don’t exceed your planned spend.
Key Takeaway

A resource monitor links measured credit usage to automated actions, making budgets enforceable rather than advisory.

screens.title: Creating a Resource Monitor
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a resource monitor requires specifying a few key properties that define its behavior. The most important are CREDIT_QUOTA and FREQUENCY. CREDIT_QUOTA is the maximum credits allowed in the chosen period, and FREQUENCY sets whether the quota applies daily, weekly, monthly, yearly, or across all time. You can also supply START_TIMESTAMP and END_TIMESTAMP to bound the monitor to a project window. A monitor supports TRIGGERS that react when consumption hits a percentage of the quota. Below is a typical creation command used in the lab: create a daily monitor with a five-credit quota and triggers at 50, 75 and 100 percent where 100 percent suspends the warehouse. Remember to replace placeholder email addresses and validate that the role creating the monitor has the right privileges. A common error is omitting START_TIMESTAMP when you intended the monitor to be active immediately; using START_TIMESTAMP = 'IMMEDIATE' avoids that mistake. After creation, use SHOW RESOURCE MONITORS to inspect CURRENT_CREDITS and STATE. Practice: copy the example, change the quota, and run SHOW RESOURCE MONITORS to confirm the monitor appears. Creating a Resource Monitor means define credit_quota, frequency, optional period bounds, and triggers to specify notifications and suspensions.. In practical terms, sql syntax and important properties. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR
keyIdea.text: Define CREDIT_QUOTA, FREQUENCY, optional period bounds, and TRIGGERS to specify notifications and suspensions.

content.html:
Process › Creating a Resource Monitor
Key properties explained
  • CREDIT_QUOTA: Maximum credits for the chosen FREQUENCY.
  • FREQUENCY: DAILY, WEEKLY, MONTHLY, YEARLY, or ALL_TIME.
  • START/END_TIMESTAMP: Optional bounds for active period.
  • TRIGGERS: Define actions at percentage thresholds.
Pro tip
Test monitor behavior in a non-production role before applying SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE in production.
Example SQL
CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR my_daily_monitor
    WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = 5
    FREQUENCY = DAILY
    START_TIMESTAMP = 'IMMEDIATE'
    TRIGGERS
        ON 50 PERCENT DO NOTIFY EMAIL 'your_email@example.com'
        ON 75 PERCENT DO NOTIFY EMAIL 'your_email@example.com'
        ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND;
This example notifies at 50% and 75%, then suspends at 100%. Use SHOW RESOURCE MONITORS to confirm creation and to view CURRENT_CREDITS and STATE.
Key Takeaway

Define clear quotas and test triggers so monitors act as intended without unintended suspension of critical workloads.

screens.title: Triggers: NOTIFY vs SUSPEND vs SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE
screens.narratorSegment: Triggers are where a monitor moves from passive measurement to active control. NOTIFY will send an email to configured addresses; it is useful for early warnings and human review. SUSPEND will stop warehouses from being resumed further in the current period, but it may let already-running queries finish; it is a softer stop. SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE forcibly suspends warehouses and cancels running queries, which is useful to halt costs quickly but can disrupt in-flight work. A typical tiered setup uses NOTIFY at 50 or 75 percent so teams can investigate, and SUSPEND or SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE at 100 percent to enforce the quota. A common misconception is to use only NOTIFY for critical production workloads; notifications alone do not prevent further accrual. Consider the business impact: if you must avoid any additional run-time costs, SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE is appropriate but should be tested first. Example: for a non-critical dev warehouse, NOTIFY at intermediate thresholds and SUSPEND at 100% may be acceptable. For a billing-limited account, SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE at 100% prevents overspend immediately. Ending thought: pick triggers by balancing cost control with operational risk and always test them in a sandbox.

keyIdea.title: Trigger selection
keyIdea.text: Use NOTIFY for warnings, SUSPEND to stop future resumes, and SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE to cancel running work and halt credit use immediately.

content.html:
Comparison › Triggers
NOTIFY
Sends email alerts at configured percentages. Best for early warning and investigation without immediate action.
Use when teams need context before action.
SUSPEND
Prevents warehouses from being resumed further in the current period but may allow running queries to finish.
A softer enforcement suited to less-critical workloads.
SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE
Immediately suspends warehouses and cancels running queries, stopping credit accrual at once.
Powerful but disruptive; always test first.
Tiered trigger strategy
Notify at 50% and 75% for visibility, then suspend or suspend immediate at 100% for enforcement.
Misuse warning
Relying solely on notifications for critical budgets risks ongoing overspend; pair notifications with enforcement where needed.
Key Takeaway

Match trigger severity to business risk: notify early, suspend for control, suspend immediate for strict enforcement.

screens.title: Assigning Monitors to Warehouses or Account
screens.narratorSegment: You assign monitors to one or more warehouses or set their level to ACCOUNT to apply an overarching quota. Assigning to individual warehouses gives you granular control per workload, which is useful when development, ETL, and reporting workloads have different tolerance for suspension. Using ACCOUNT level provides a single budget for the whole account, which is helpful for overall cost governance. Use ALTER RESOURCE MONITOR to set warehouses, or use ALTER RESOURCE MONITOR... SET LEVEL = ACCOUNT to change scope. For example, ALTER RESOURCE MONITOR my_monitor SET WAREHOUSES = (DEV_WH, ETL_WH); attaches the monitor to those warehouses. A common misconception is that assigning a monitor to both individual warehouses and the account stacks quotas; in practice you should design quotas so they don't unintentionally double-restrict normal operations. Best practice: a tiered approach where an account-level monitor enforces a global budget and warehouse-level monitors handle workload-specific thresholds. Always communicate monitor assignments to stakeholders so unexpected suspensions do not surprise active teams. To verify, run SHOW RESOURCE MONITORS and inspect assigned warehouses and the CURRENT_CREDITS. As a reflective question, which combination of account and warehouse monitors would provide both safety and operational flexibility in your environment?

keyIdea.title: Granularity matters
keyIdea.text: Assign monitors to warehouses for targeted control, or set LEVEL = ACCOUNT for account-wide budgets; combine them carefully to avoid over-restriction.

content.html:
Process Flow › Assigning monitors
Granularity trade-offs
  • Warehouse-level: Targeted quotas for dev, ETL, or reporting.
  • Account-level: Single budget across all warehouses for overall governance.
  • Combined: Use account monitor plus selective warehouse monitors for layered protection.
Communicate assignments to stakeholders and avoid overlapping quotas that block legitimate operations.
Example ALTER commands
ALTER RESOURCE MONITOR my_monitor SET WAREHOUSES = (DEV_WH, ETL_WH);

ALTER RESOURCE MONITOR my_monitor SET LEVEL = ACCOUNT;

SHOW RESOURCE MONITORS;
Use SHOW RESOURCE MONITORS to confirm assignments, current credits, and monitor state after applying changes.
Key Takeaway

Choose assignment granularity to balance protection and operational flexibility, and verify settings with SHOW commands.

screens.title: Credits: Compute, Storage, and Cloud Services
screens.narratorSegment: Credits are Snowflake's billing unit and can be consumed in three primary ways: compute, storage, and cloud services. Compute credits are consumed by virtual warehouses while they run; larger warehouse sizes use more credits per hour. Storage credits accumulate as data is persisted, including time travel and fail-safe retention. Cloud services credits are used for account-level operations such as metadata management, security services, and internal optimizations. Understanding these categories is crucial because resource monitors primarily control compute via warehouse suspension, while storage growth and cloud services require different cost-management strategies. For example, a sudden spike in query execution will show up immediately in WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY and can be controlled with a monitor. In contrast, a storage spike from large data retention appears in STORAGE_USAGE and needs retention policy or data lifecycle changes. A common misconception is to assume a monitor will cap storage spend — it will not. The practical implication is to pair monitors for compute with regular storage reviews using ACCOUNT_USAGE views and lifecycle policies. Consider a workload with steady compute but growing storage; you might use a warehouse monitor plus storage housekeeping to manage total spend. What would you inspect first: warehouse meters or storage usage, and why?

keyIdea.title: Three credit types
keyIdea.text: Compute credits drive most short-term variability and are controlled by monitors; storage and services need lifecycle and governance controls.

content.html:
Definition › Credit Types
Compute credits
Consumed by virtual warehouses while executing queries or loads. Use monitors to limit these credits.
Inspect: WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY
Storage credits
Accrue as data is stored, including time travel and fail-safe. Manage with retention and cleanup policies.
Inspect: STORAGE_USAGE, DATABASE_STORAGE_USAGE_HISTORY
Cloud services
Account-level operations and metadata management consume credits used for services and optimizations.
Inspect: ACCOUNT_USAGE service views
Example contrast
A long-running analytical query raises compute credits immediately, whereas adding a large dataset increases storage credits over time.
Misconception check
A monitor will not directly reduce storage costs; you must apply retention or archive policies for that.
Key Takeaway

Match your control tools to the credit type: monitors for compute, lifecycle policies for storage, governance for services.

screens.title: Using ACCOUNT_USAGE to Analyze Consumption
screens.narratorSegment: Snowflake provides the ACCOUNT_USAGE schema in the SNOWFLAKE shared database to help you analyze historical consumption. Important views include WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY for warehouse credits over time, QUERY_HISTORY for query-level details, and STORAGE_USAGE for storage counts. These views let you find trends, peak hours, and which warehouses drive costs. A common investigative query aggregates daily credits by warehouse over the last month; it is invaluable for spotting cost drivers and validating monitor effectiveness. The sample query returns a date, the warehouse name, and total credits used per day. One practical tip: filter by START_TIME to limit the date range and use GROUP BY to focus on the warehouses you care about. A typical misconception is expecting QUERY_HISTORY to directly show aggregated warehouse credits; query history shows per-query details, whereas WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY gives aggregated credit consumption. Use both together: metering for totals, query history to find expensive statements. After running the sample query, look for sustained high-credit days and correlate them with job schedules or ETL windows. Which warehouse shows the largest daily spikes and what process runs there? Using ACCOUNT_USAGE to Analyze Consumption means use warehouse_metering_history for credit totals and query_history to pinpoint expensive queries; combine both for root-cause analysis.. In practical terms, key views and a sample query for daily warehouse usage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › ACCOUNT_USAGE analysis
Key views
  • WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY — credit consumption by warehouse and time.
  • QUERY_HISTORY — statements, durations, and resource usage per query.
  • STORAGE_USAGE — historical storage totals by database and table.
Combine metering history for totals and query history for root-cause analysis of expensive statements.
Sample query: daily warehouse credits
SELECT
  TO_DATE(START_TIME) AS usage_date,
  WAREHOUSE_NAME,
  SUM(CREDITS_USED) AS total_credits_used
FROM
  SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY
WHERE
  START_TIME >= DATEADD(month, -1, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP BY
  1, 2
ORDER BY
  1, 2;
Run this to produce a daily breakdown of credits by warehouse for the last month. Use the results to target monitors or investigate costly queries.
Key Takeaway

Account usage views are the source of truth for consumption analysis; use them to validate monitor settings and to find cost drivers.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity › Lab Walkthrough
Steps
  1. Create a small test warehouse as ACCOUNTADMIN.
  2. Create a daily resource monitor with triggers and a small quota.
  3. Assign the monitor to the test warehouse.
  4. Run a long-running query repeatedly to consume credits.
  5. Watch notifications and monitor state, then clean up test objects.
Safety: test suspend immediate only in a sandbox to understand the effect on running queries.
Starter commands
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
CREATE WAREHOUSE TEST_RM_WH WITH WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'XSMALL' AUTO_SUSPEND = 60 AUTO_RESUME = TRUE;

CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR my_daily_monitor
  WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = 5
  FREQUENCY = DAILY
  START_TIMESTAMP = 'IMMEDIATE'
  TRIGGERS
    ON 50 PERCENT DO NOTIFY EMAIL 'your_email@example.com'
    ON 75 PERCENT DO NOTIFY EMAIL 'your_email@example.com'
    ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND;

ALTER WAREHOUSE TEST_RM_WH SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = my_daily_monitor;
Simulation tip

Run an aggregation over the sample TPCH data repeatedly to consume credits. Monitor email for NOTIFY and check SHOW RESOURCE MONITORS to observe effects.

screens.title: Pitfalls and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Many organizations underuse resource monitors or configure them in ways that reduce their effectiveness. Common mistakes include not setting monitors at all, giving quotas that are too high to be meaningful, relying only on notifications for mission-critical budgets, and failing to revisit quotas as usage patterns change. For example, setting a month-long quota for a daily cost problem is ineffective. Another frequent issue is using SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE in production without testing, which can break running workloads unexpectedly. Best practices mitigate these problems: adopt a tiered approach with an account-level monitor plus targeted warehouse monitors, use tiered triggers (notify early, suspend at final threshold), test suspend behaviors in a sandbox, and regularly review ACCOUNT_USAGE reports to tune quotas. Also, communicate monitor changes to teams so that suspensions are expected and can be coordinated with stakeholders. Finally, include monitor checks in your operational runbooks and dashboards so alerts are actionable. A simple question to guide change: which monitor will prevent your highest daily cost spike without interrupting critical nightly jobs? Common Mistakes › Pitfalls & Best Practices
Frequent mistakes
  • Not creating monitors or setting quotas too high to be effective.
  • Using notifications only for critical budgets and not enforcing suspension.
  • Applying SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE in production without sandbox testing.
  • Ignoring ACCOUNT_USAGE and not tuning quotas over time.
Best practices
  • Use account-level plus warehouse-level monitors for layered protection.
  • Tier triggers: notify early, suspend when necessary.
  • Test suspend effects in a non-production environment.
  • Schedule regular reviews of ACCOUNT_USAGE to adjust quotas.
Key Takeaway

Treat monitors as part of an ongoing governance cycle: configure, test, monitor, and tune to keep costs predictable without disrupting essential work.

Check Your Understanding › Assessment Scenario
Assessment example
Create a monthly monitor for ETL_WH with 100 credit quota, notify at 80% to data_ops, and suspend immediately at 100%.
CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR etl_monthly_monitor

screens.title: Tiered Monitor Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: A robust monitoring strategy uses tiers: an account-level monitor protects overall budget, and targeted warehouse monitors handle workload-specific risks. The account-level monitor defines a broad cap — for example, monthly spending for the entire organization. Warehouse-level monitors provide finer control and let teams establish quotas appropriate to their workload type. For instance, an ETL warehouse might have a monthly quota with SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE at 100% to avoid extra billing, while a BI reporting warehouse might use softer controls to avoid interrupting dashboards. This hierarchical setup avoids a single point of failure and provides both emergency stop and fine-grained control. One misconception is thinking two overlapping monitors will always stack to stricter protection; overlaps can create unintended freezes if thresholds are too tight across both levels. Best practice is to design non-conflicting quotas where account quotas allow reasonable aggregate usage while warehouses enforce local limits for runaway jobs. Regularly review ACCOUNT_USAGE to adjust both tiers as usage patterns evolve and ensure thresholds remain aligned with business priorities. Consider which workloads need stricter limits and why, then design quotas accordingly. Tiered Monitor Strategy means combine an account-level monitor for global budget with warehouse monitors for workload-specific enforcement, and tune to avoid conflicting restrictions.. In practical terms, account-level guardrail plus workload-level controls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Best Practice › Tiered Monitor Strategy
Account-level
A high-level budget cap for the entire account, useful as a final safety net.
Example: Monthly quota to prevent runaway total spend.
Warehouse-level
Targeted quotas for ETL, dev, or reporting to balance cost and availability.
Example: ETL_WH with lower daily quota and SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE at final threshold.
Governance
Regular review cycles and communication with teams to tune quotas and avoid surprises.
Example: Monthly review of WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY and quota adjustments.
Key Takeaway

Use layered monitors and review data regularly to maintain cost control without harming critical operations.

fullNarratorScript:
In cloud billing, visibility is the first line of defence. In this lesson you will learn what a Snowflake Resource Monitor does, how credits measure cost across compute, storage and cloud services, and why combining quotas with automated triggers prevents runaway spend. We will ground this with concrete S Q L commands you can run, a short simulation you can reproduce in a sandbox, and the ACCOUNT_USAGE views you use to analyze consumption. You’ll see how a tiered approach — account-level monitors plus targeted warehouse monitors — gives both budget-level protection and workload-level control. A practical example: if a long-running ETL keeps an X-SMALL warehouse running, a daily quota and a suspend trigger stop further credits from accruing until someone reviews the workload. Common pitfalls we’ll avoid include relying only on email notifications, using overly large quotas that are ineffective, and failing to test suspend actions in non-production. By the end you will be able to create a monitor, assign it, read metering history, and choose sensible triggers. Consider: what workload in your environment would you protect first and why?

These objectives focus your practice so you can manage Snowflake costs with confidence. First, you will be able to explain why a resource monitor is essential: it maps credit consumption to guardrails and prevents surprise bills. A concrete example is how a daily quota can keep a long-running development warehouse from consuming unbounded credits overnight. Second, you will configure and manage resource monitors using S Q L, including defining a credit quota and frequency, and assigning monitors to one or more warehouses. You’ll practice creating triggers that notify or suspend a warehouse. Third, you will differentiate the types of credit consumption: compute for warehouses, storage for persisted data and time travel, and cloud services for account metadata and optimizations. Finally, you will query the ACCOUNT_USAGE schema to analyze usage and set up alerts: reading WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY to find high-consuming warehouses and using SHOW RESOURCE MONITORS to inspect monitor state. Each objective links a practical task with a measurable result so you can demonstrate competency at the end of the lab.

In this practice-focused view we connect each objective to a lab action. For explaining resource monitors, you will describe a monitor that suspends a development warehouse at a daily quota and justify the choice. For configuration, you will write CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR S Q L, set triggers, and attach the monitor to a test warehouse. For credit types, you will query ACCOUNT_USAGE to separate compute credits from storage growth, demonstrating how storage charges grow differently than compute. For analysis and alerts, you will run the WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY example query to produce a daily breakdown, then interpret which warehouses to throttle or increase capacity for. Each competency requires evidence: a monitor created in a sandbox, a query that shows peak hours, and a short rationale for trigger thresholds. This learning-objective screen ties actions to outcomes so you can confidently complete the hands-on activity and the assessment question that follows.

A Resource Monitor is a Snowflake object that measures credit consumption and enforces controls when thresholds are reached. Think of it as an automated budget guardrail: you set a CREDIT_QUOTA for a time period, and the monitor counts consumed credits against that quota. The practical reason this exists is billing behavior — compute credits accrue while warehouses run, storage grows over time, and cloud services use credits for account-level operations. A concrete example helps. Imagine a development warehouse that accidentally stays active overnight during a large data load. A daily resource monitor with a small CREDIT_QUOTA will notify at intermediate percentages and then suspend the warehouse when the quota is reached, halting further cost accrual. One common misconception is that resource monitors stop all billing automatically across storage and services; they primarily control compute consumption for assigned warehouses or the account level via SUSPEND actions. Storage and cloud services still accrue unless you explicitly manage those costs separately. Takeaway: resource monitors translate credit tracking into enforced actions, but they must be combined with usage analysis and design to be effective. Which small workload in your environment would you protect first and why?

Creating a resource monitor requires specifying a few key properties that define its behavior. The most important are CREDIT_QUOTA and FREQUENCY. CREDIT_QUOTA is the maximum credits allowed in the chosen period, and FREQUENCY sets whether the quota applies daily, weekly, monthly, yearly, or across all time. You can also supply START_TIMESTAMP and END_TIMESTAMP to bound the monitor to a project window. A monitor supports TRIGGERS that react when consumption hits a percentage of the quota. Below is a typical creation command used in the lab: create a daily monitor with a five-credit quota and triggers at 50, 75 and 100 percent where 100 percent suspends the warehouse. Remember to replace placeholder email addresses and validate that the role creating the monitor has the right privileges. A common error is omitting START_TIMESTAMP when you intended the monitor to be active immediately; using START_TIMESTAMP = 'IMMEDIATE' avoids that mistake. After creation, use SHOW RESOURCE MONITORS to inspect CURRENT_CREDITS and STATE. Practice: copy the example, change the quota, and run SHOW RESOURCE MONITORS to confirm the monitor appears. Creating a Resource Monitor means define credit_quota, frequency, optional period bounds, and triggers to specify notifications and suspensions.. In practical terms, sql syntax and important properties. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Triggers are where a monitor moves from passive measurement to active control. NOTIFY will send an email to configured addresses; it is useful for early warnings and human review. SUSPEND will stop warehouses from being resumed further in the current period, but it may let already-running queries finish; it is a softer stop. SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE forcibly suspends warehouses and cancels running queries, which is useful to halt costs quickly but can disrupt in-flight work. A typical tiered setup uses NOTIFY at 50 or 75 percent so teams can investigate, and SUSPEND or SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE at 100 percent to enforce the quota. A common misconception is to use only NOTIFY for critical production workloads; notifications alone do not prevent further accrual. Consider the business impact: if you must avoid any additional run-time costs, SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE is appropriate but should be tested first. Example: for a non-critical dev warehouse, NOTIFY at intermediate thresholds and SUSPEND at 100% may be acceptable. For a billing-limited account, SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE at 100% prevents overspend immediately. Ending thought: pick triggers by balancing cost control with operational risk and always test them in a sandbox.

You assign monitors to one or more warehouses or set their level to ACCOUNT to apply an overarching quota. Assigning to individual warehouses gives you granular control per workload, which is useful when development, ETL, and reporting workloads have different tolerance for suspension. Using ACCOUNT level provides a single budget for the whole account, which is helpful for overall cost governance. Use ALTER RESOURCE MONITOR to set warehouses, or use ALTER RESOURCE MONITOR... SET LEVEL = ACCOUNT to change scope. For example, ALTER RESOURCE MONITOR my_monitor SET WAREHOUSES = (DEV_WH, ETL_WH); attaches the monitor to those warehouses. A common misconception is that assigning a monitor to both individual warehouses and the account stacks quotas; in practice you should design quotas so they don't unintentionally double-restrict normal operations. Best practice: a tiered approach where an account-level monitor enforces a global budget and warehouse-level monitors handle workload-specific thresholds. Always communicate monitor assignments to stakeholders so unexpected suspensions do not surprise active teams. To verify, run SHOW RESOURCE MONITORS and inspect assigned warehouses and the CURRENT_CREDITS. As a reflective question, which combination of account and warehouse monitors would provide both safety and operational flexibility in your environment?

Credits are Snowflake's billing unit and can be consumed in three primary ways: compute, storage, and cloud services. Compute credits are consumed by virtual warehouses while they run; larger warehouse sizes use more credits per hour. Storage credits accumulate as data is persisted, including time travel and fail-safe retention. Cloud services credits are used for account-level operations such as metadata management, security services, and internal optimizations. Understanding these categories is crucial because resource monitors primarily control compute via warehouse suspension, while storage growth and cloud services require different cost-management strategies. For example, a sudden spike in query execution will show up immediately in WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY and can be controlled with a monitor. In contrast, a storage spike from large data retention appears in STORAGE_USAGE and needs retention policy or data lifecycle changes. A common misconception is to assume a monitor will cap storage spend — it will not. The practical implication is to pair monitors for compute with regular storage reviews using ACCOUNT_USAGE views and lifecycle policies. Consider a workload with steady compute but growing storage; you might use a warehouse monitor plus storage housekeeping to manage total spend. What would you inspect first: warehouse meters or storage usage, and why?

Snowflake provides the ACCOUNT_USAGE schema in the SNOWFLAKE shared database to help you analyze historical consumption. Many organizations underuse resource monitors or configure them in ways that reduce their effectiveness. Common mistakes include not setting monitors at all, giving quotas that are too high to be meaningful, relying only on notifications for mission-critical budgets, and failing to revisit quotas as usage patterns change. For example, setting a month-long quota for a daily cost problem is ineffective. Another frequent issue is using SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE in production without testing, which can break running workloads unexpectedly. Best practices mitigate these problems: adopt a tiered approach with an account-level monitor plus targeted warehouse monitors, use tiered triggers (notify early, suspend at final threshold), test suspend behaviors in a sandbox, and regularly review ACCOUNT_USAGE reports to tune quotas. Also, communicate monitor changes to teams so that suspensions are expected and can be coordinated with stakeholders. Finally, include monitor checks in your operational runbooks and dashboards so alerts are actionable. A simple question to guide change: which monitor will prevent your highest daily cost spike without interrupting critical nightly jobs? A robust monitoring strategy uses tiers: an account-level monitor protects overall budget, and targeted warehouse monitors handle workload-specific risks. The account-level monitor defines a broad cap — for example, monthly spending for the entire organization. Warehouse-level monitors provide finer control and let teams establish quotas appropriate to their workload type. For instance, an ETL warehouse might have a monthly quota with SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE at 100% to avoid extra billing, while a BI reporting warehouse might use softer controls to avoid interrupting dashboards. This hierarchical setup avoids a single point of failure and provides both emergency stop and fine-grained control. One misconception is thinking two overlapping monitors will always stack to stricter protection; overlaps can create unintended freezes if thresholds are too tight across both levels. Best practice is to design non-conflicting quotas where account quotas allow reasonable aggregate usage while warehouses enforce local limits for runaway jobs. Regularly review ACCOUNT_USAGE to adjust both tiers as usage patterns evolve and ensure thresholds remain aligned with business priorities. Consider which workloads need stricter limits and why, then design quotas accordingly.
